item.title: The Purpose of Laughter
item.description:
Laughter

The Purpose of Laughter

Across societies and cultures, laughter is a universally recognized language.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • A new review explains laughter as more than a reaction to humor.
  • The brain uses two partly separate systems for laughter.
  • One System is for spontaneous emotional outbursts.
  • Another is for deliberate social expression.

Long before humans built cities, wrote laws, or argued about politics, they laughed. Across societies and cultures, laughter is a universally recognized language.

A new review, “The Neural Basis of Laughter,” asks what happens in the brain when this ancient sound breaks through the body. The paper argues that laughter has two purposes. One relates to emotion, play, bonding, and the body’s deep social instincts. The other belongs to conversation, timing, manners, and voluntary control. The laugh that erupts from the belly and the laugh used to smooth a conversation may sound related, but the brain appears to build them through different routes.

A Sound Older Than Speech

Spontaneous laughter is the kind that bursts out during play, delight, embarrassment, or contagion. Someone else laughs, and the sound pulls us along. This type of laughter has ancient roots. Other animals produce play sounds that help signal friendliness and prevent rough play from turning into aggression. Human laughter also carries that social message.

The review places this spontaneous laughter in a network centered on emotional and social regions of the brain. One important hub is the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in emotion, bodily awareness, social behavior, and pain regulation. When doctors have stimulated this area during clinical procedures, some patients have smiled, laughed, felt mirth, or experienced a sense of relief. In some cases, stimulation even produced laughter during negative memories, as if the brain had opened a hidden door to positive feelings.

The temporal pole, another region linked to social and emotional meaning, also plays a role in this type of laughter. Stimulation there can produce laughter that feels natural and contagious. Together, these two regions seem to form a gateway for laughter that carries feeling, bodily change, and social warmth.

This system also reaches deeper structures in the brain that help shape the physical act of laughing. These areas help create the whole event of laughter: the breath, the face, the sound, the bodily rush, and the feeling that laughter has taken possession of us.

The Social Laugh

Humans also laugh when nothing is especially funny. We laugh to show agreement, to ease tension, to keep a conversation moving, or to signal that we understand the social rules of the moment. This laugh belongs to culture as much as biology. It must fit the timing of speech: at the end of a sentence, after a joke, during an awkward pause, or when politeness demands a signal of warmth.

The paper argues that this voluntary laughter depends more on motor and speech-related regions. These include areas in the brain involved in the mouth, tongue, face, and voice. When doctors stimulate these areas, patients may smile, produce laughter-like sounds, or experience changes in speech. Often, the laughter lacks genuine amusement. It resembles the machinery of expression without the emotional drive behind it.

Spontaneous laughter tends to be more stereotyped and less shaped by the tongue and mouth. Voluntary laughter, by contrast, can be sculpted. It can be polite, ironic, strategic, charming, or forced. A person can also laugh simply because the conversation requires it, and the brain seems to make a distinction between the two laughs.

When Laughter Becomes a Symptom

The paper’s clinical examples reveal how powerful this distinction can be. Some people experience gelastic seizures, sudden episodes of laughter caused by abnormal brain activity. The laughter may sound natural, even when it does not match the person’s emotional state.

In another condition called cataplexy, often associated with narcolepsy, strong emotions can trigger a sudden loss of muscle tone. Laughter is one of the most common triggers. Cataplexy seems to involve the loss of neurons important for wakefulness and bodily control.

Then there is pseudobulbar affect, sometimes called pathological laughing and crying. People with this condition may laugh or cry abruptly, intensely, and out of proportion to what they feel. It can occur after brain injury, stroke, or neurodegenerative disease. Such cases show that laughter depends on delicate coordination between emotional networks and motor control systems. When that coordination breaks, laughter can become detached from the inner life it usually expresses.

To Laugh Is to Bond

Shared laughter has also been shown to raise pain thresholds. The anterior cingulate connects with brain regions involved in descending pain control, including pathways that can dampen the emotional burden of pain.

This gives laughter an almost medicinal quality. It binds groups while also changing how the body feels. Across human history, a group that could play, bond, and endure discomfort together had an advantage. Humans do not merely think together. We have the capability to regulate one another’s nervous systems.

Modern people often treat laughter as entertainment, a pleasant side effect of jokes, comedy, and amusement. However, this paper shows that laughter becomes a bridge between ancient mammalian play and modern human conversation.

To understand laughter is to understand one of humanity’s earliest social technologies. Before contracts, before alphabets, before philosophy, there was this shared sound. The brain built laughter to connect fragile creatures to one another, to soften pain, to signal belonging, and to turn the solitary nervous system into something that thrives in society.

item.title: When Feeling Better Doesn't Feel Like Yourself
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

When Feeling Better Doesn't Feel Like Yourself

Symptom relief can also change how a person experiences their own mind.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Psychiatric medications can ease symptoms while also changing how people experience emotions.
  • Long-standing symptoms can become part of identity, blurring the line between disorder and self.
  • These changes vary widely and often improve with time, a dose change, or a new medication.
Source: Alonso Reyes / Unsplash

For as long as she could remember, there had always been a soundtrack in her mind. Not a hallucination, just a song playing somewhere in the background, changing every few minutes, interrupted by unfinished thoughts, imaginary conversations, grocery lists, and memories surfacing without invitation. The mental noise was so constant that she never questioned it. It was simply how her brain worked.

A few days after starting medication for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), something changed.

The music was gone.

So were many of the thoughts competing for her attention. For the first time, her mind felt quiet. She could finish a task without wandering away from it. She could read a page without starting over three times.

By every practical measure, the treatment was working. But instead of relief, she felt something she hadn't expected.

"I don't feel like myself anymore."

When the world feels different

Psychiatric medications don't just reduce symptoms. They can also change how people experience their thoughts, emotions, and even their relationship with the world around them.

Sometimes those changes are exactly what treatment is meant to achieve. A person with ADHD may discover what sustained attention feels like for the first time. Someone with severe anxiety may notice an unfamiliar sense of calm. A patient recovering from depression may no longer wake up with the same emotional weight that had become part of everyday life.

Other changes are less welcome.

Some people taking antidepressants describe emotional blunting. The deepest sadness fades, but so does the intensity of joy, excitement, or love. Others report feeling emotionally distant, as though life is happening behind a pane of glass.

Patients taking stimulant medication for ADHD sometimes say their thoughts are more organized but also less spontaneous, leaving them worried that they have become less creative or less like themselves.

These experiences are highly individual. Many people never experience them, and when they do occur, their intensity varies widely. In some cases they improve after the first weeks of treatment, after a dose adjustment, or after switching to another medication.

But while they last, they can fundamentally change how a person experiences daily life.

Time shapes perception

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder. Its symptoms begin in childhood, even if the diagnosis comes decades later. Adults diagnosed later in life may have spent their entire lives with distractibility, racing thoughts, impulsivity, or constant mental noise. There is no "before" against which to compare treatment. A quieter mind is not a return to a familiar state. It is a completely new experience.

Other psychiatric disorders follow a different course. Most people with depression, anxiety disorders, or obsessive-compulsive disorder can remember a time before the symptoms appeared. There is a reference point, a version of themselves that existed before the illness.

But that distinction can become less clear as time passes. When symptoms persist for years, they gradually become woven into everyday life. People adapt to them, make sense of themselves through them, and stop noticing how much their way of thinking, feeling, or reacting has changed. By the time treatment begins, separating what belongs to the disorder from what feels like part of one's own personality may no longer be straightforward.

That may help explain why some treatment-related changes feel so unsettling. Patients are not simply adjusting to the absence of symptoms. They are trying to make sense of a different way of experiencing their own mind.

The changes we don't always measure

Psychiatric treatment is often evaluated by what improves. Clinicians look at whether depressive symptoms decrease, whether anxiety becomes more manageable, or whether attention and daily functioning improve.

But some of the changes that matter most to patients are harder to capture.

Emotional blunting is one example. Some people taking antidepressants or antipsychotics describe a feeling that their emotional world has become muted. They may feel less connected to experiences that once felt meaningful or notice that emotions no longer have the same intensity they used to.

These experiences are not always reflected in clinical assessments.

Finding the person beyond the symptoms

When a person starts psychiatric treatment, the focus is usually on what happens after medication begins. But understanding what life was like before the symptoms, and what daily life could look like without them, is just as important.

Over time, symptoms can become familiar. They influence choices, relationships, and daily routines. So when treatment changes these patterns, the result can feel confusing because the person is not only experiencing fewer symptoms. They are also adjusting to a different way of living.

Understanding where these experiences came from can make these changes easier to interpret. A life without certain symptoms may feel unfamiliar at first, especially when those symptoms have been present for years. But unfamiliar does not always mean wrong.

item.title: 'Purity Culture' Increases Sexual Shame and Problems in Sex
item.description:
Sex

'Purity Culture' Increases Sexual Shame and Problems in Sex

Those raised in purity culture suffer psychologically and sexually.

Posted August 3, 2026

We don’t hear much about purity culture anymore. It had its media moment in the 1990s. But purity culture is still integral to the sexually conservative. Purity culture views sex as immoral and sinful outside of heterosexual marriage.

Meanwhile, data from the National Survey of Family Growth, an ongoing study of American behavior, show that by age 30, more than 90 percent of Americans engage in premarital sex. “Almost all Americans have sex before marrying.” The actual proportion is probably higher than 90 percent. Many people won't admit to stigmatized behavior, and for young evangelicals, sex outside heterosexual marriage is highly stigmatized.

Evangelical young people hear one message about sex, but do something else. A recent study shows that this causes cognitive dissonance and shame that may torpedo sexual satisfaction.

The Study

Researchers at the University of Texas, Austin, surveyed the sexual attitudes and emotions of 85 students. Fundamentalist Christianity is popular in Texas. Many study participants identified as Evangelicals. At home and at church, they had first-hand experience of purity culture. Compared with other students, those raised with purity imperatives expressed significantly more sexual shame (p = 0.0008). Those feelings interfered with their sexual function (p = 0.001) and satisfaction (p = 0.001).

The Tenets of Purity

Purity culture draws its directives from the Christian Bible, especially from these two passages:

“Each man should have sexual relations with his own wife, and each woman with her own husband.” (1 Corinthians 7)

“Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the adulterer and all the sexually immoral.” (Hebrews 3:14)

Expanding on these verses, purity culture advocates:

• Traditional gender roles. Men work. Women remain at home and raise children.

• No self-sexing. Solo sex is absolutely forbidden.

• No dating. It encourages premarital sex. Spouses should meet and court at church.

• Spiritual awakening. Abstinence from sex opens the heart and soul.

Those who embrace purity culture often take virginity pledges, vowing to remain virgins until their wedding nights. Before marriage, they socialize at purity balls and declare their sexual abstinence by wearing purity rings.

Research by the Institute for Family Studies, an organization that tracks religious Christians' attitudes and practices, found that from 2008 to 2018, more than three-quarters of unmarried young adult Evangelicals—86 percent of the women and 82 percent of the men—reported partner sex. That rate is somewhat lower than other young Americans, but it shows that the large majority of young Evangelicals ignore religious calls for premarital abstinence.

And more than half the women (57 percent) and two-thirds of the men (65 percent) said they’d had three or more partners.

The Contraceptive Connection

Some research shows that as religiosity increases, use of birth control pills decreases. Ministers have trumpeted this finding. Less pill use, they say, means less sex.

But is The Pill a good indicator of sexual behavior? University of Texas, Austin, researchers investigated the relationship between religiosity and young sexually conservative women’s experience of premarital intercourse. The researchers mined data from the Relationship Dynamics and Social Life study based at Indiana University, which tracks young adult sexuality. The researchers found that, yes, as religiosity increases, use of The Pill decreases. But as religiosity increases, the young women are much more likely to use condoms.

Why the preference for condoms over The Pill? It takes considerable planning to use birth control pills: doctor visits, taking a pill daily, refilling prescriptions. It also takes planning to use an IUD or diaphragm. Young-adult Evangelical women shy away from planning for sex. But when they find themselves undressing with young men—and most do—they opt for condoms, which require less planning. They buy condoms over-the-counter and hide them in their purses.

Changing Attitudes

San Diego State University researchers tracked young adults’ attitudes toward premarital sex since World War II. They used meta-analysis, a standard statistical technique, to pool the results of 530 small studies as though they’d all been part of one large one. The larger the study, the more reliable its results. The 530 reports included 269,649 participants, a huge number, which lends credence to the findings. The meta-analysis showed that young adults’ sexual attitudes and behavior have changed dramatically over the past 75 years, with the largest shift occurring among girls and young women. They have become increasingly accepting of premarital sex, with approval increasing from 12 percent in 1949 to 73 percent in the twenty-first century. Again, the actual percentages are probably higher.

Cognitive Dissonance

Being told to act in a certain way that’s “moral,” then acting in another that’s “immoral” produces cognitive dissonance, a clash of values. Cognitive dissonance about sexual abstinence often causes shame, embarrassment, and humiliation, especially when parents, teachers, or peers learn they’re having premarital sex—and berate them.

Shame causes stress and anxiety, which release the stress hormone, cortisol. It directs blood away from the central body, including the genitals, and out to the limbs for escape or self-defense. Less blood in the genitals impairs sexual function. Stress is notorious for interfering with sexual pleasure and satisfaction. In pursuit of religious grace, purity culture makes young people feel stressed and ashamed, which the UT study shows interferes with their sexual function and erotic satisfaction.

Many religions prohibit premarital sex—Catholicism, Islam, Orthodox Judaism, and many Protestant denominations also frown on it. But on this issue, Evangelicals have been the most vocal, which attracts the most media and research attention.

Religious people are free to believe whatever their religions teach. But it’s a shame for any institution, religious or secular, to demand behavior that, culturally speaking, is close to impossible, behavior that causes its members shame, and may well derail their sexual function and pleasure.

item.title: Why Is the Mother-Daughter Relationship so Tricky?
item.description:
Parenting

Why Is the Mother-Daughter Relationship so Tricky?

Both mothers and daughters get confused about their dynamics.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Mothers and daughters who are close may also experience conflict.
  • Moms should listen to and try to understand their daughters.
  • "Suggestions" from mothers may be perceived by daughters as criticisms.

After decades of hearing about this in my consultation room and experiencing this in my own life, I must say that the mother-daughter relationship is clearly extremely complicated. It is complicated for both mothers and for daughters and for those around them who experience the tension and the joy as well as the closeness and the conflict. I have not met a single mother or daughter who described their relationship as easy, despite often describing the relationship as close and even loving.

Factors That Shape the Mother-Daughter Relationship in Adolescence and Adulthood

There are a number of factors at play in the mother-daughter relationship. The relationship becomes particularly fraught when the girls enter adolescence and are trying to develop their own unique identities separate from what their mothers may want for them, and as the daughters enter various phases of adulthood and mothers and daughters may have differing views of goals and boundaries.

When mothers have daughters, they often have a clear view of who their daughters will be in terms of aspirations and goals. As the teen years hit, daughters experiment with different identities (which is normal), and mothers often criticize and judge because they fear that their daughters are making mistakes and that their parenting has failed. This is a recipe for fighting and misunderstandings. Mothers and daughters may be looking at situations and experiencing them totally differently.

This is where listening should prevail rather than criticizing and suggesting. Sit down with your daughters. Listen to their views. Find out why the friend that you dislike may be special to her. Listen to what your daughter is saying and put aside your preconceived notions about who she should be and who she should be friends with. Please, bear in mind that you and your daughter are different people and the world needs all kinds of people. Ultimately, the most important goal is the quality of the relationship between you and your daughter, and this comes from understanding and support rather than from judgment and suggestions. Your daughter may not mirror you, and she may not be exactly who you want her to be.

As your daughter enters adulthood, you may decide to weigh in heavily about career and partner choices. You have already made these choices in your own life. It is your daughter's turn to figure out these choices. If she asks for your input, be available. If she simply wants to talk out loud, then hold this space for her and focus on listening. You want to be her go-to person rather than someone she avoids.

Managing Boundaries When Daughters Become Mothers

Another difficult stage between mothers and daughters often comes to life when the daughters raise children. It is up to the daughters to decide how much involvement they want from their moms. Your daughter will set boundaries, and, unless you want to be avoided by your daughter, then I suggest that you take her boundaries seriously. Perhaps she wants you to limit how frequently you visit or how much you gift her children. Pay attention and honor her requests. You may also want to set your own boundaries. Babysitting may not be your top priority. Discuss this so resentment doesn't build.

If there is no tension in your relationship with your daughter, then my guess is that the relationship is likely superficial. Meaningful and close relationships between mothers and daughters will have ups and downs. The trick here is to put aside judgment and do a lot of listening. It will reap many benefits.

item.title: In Group Projects: Double Down or Quit?
item.description:
Teamwork

In Group Projects: Double Down or Quit?

Should you forge ahead anyway, though some don't pull their weight?

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Getting things done in groups sometimes demands putting up with the unfairly low contribution of "slackers."
  • We designed a new decision game to study the dynamics of "pushing ahead" versus holding back in this dilemma.
  • Not getting too "bent out of shape" by those not pulling their weight emerges as a helpful lesson.

You’re part of a group—maybe family, maybe fellow investors or professionals, maybe a team of managers or employees—working together to complete a project that none of you could complete on your own. It could be a small project, like beautifying the land enclosed by a cul-de-sac shared by five homes or providing dishes for a family gathering, or a larger one, like researching and writing a report about a new product line or community center. The dynamics at work are even present on far larger scales, like determining contributions to the U.N. or N.A.T.O., or what effort individual countries contribute to fighting climate change.

Most of you are doing your best to push the project along, but a few seem to keep probing to figure out how little they can get away with doing and to what extent others will pick up the slack for them. If replacing them with others who’ll pull their weight isn’t feasible, should you keep contributing your own effort or funds, pull back to try to teach the laggards a lesson, or give up and stop throwing good money (effort) after bad?

Dilemmas of Cooperation

Both economists and psychologists have conducted thousands of studies of dilemmas of cooperation that include people in this sort of position. One of the most pervasive themes of those studies is that many people intensely dislike having others free ride on their efforts, and that cooperation often founders on the nearly ubiquitous presence, along with these detesters of free riding, of individuals who try to get away with doing less.

Studies by behavioral experimental economists establish that most individuals are inclined to contribute more the more that they know others are contributing, which seems like good news compared to the assumption that everyone is determined to contribute nothing at all. People tend, that is, to be “conditional cooperators.” However, the large majority of conditional cooperators are also “selfishly biased” in the sense that their ideal is to increase their effort roughly but not quite fully in proportion to that of others—in other words, to try to more or less keep up, yet do “just a little less” when possible. If everyone’s goal is to match others’ contributions roughly 80 or 90 cents to the dollar, the long-run result can still be a race—or at least a slow jog—to the bottom, one in which everyone’s effort slowly approaches zero as each tries to do about as much as, but just a little less than, the others.

However, it’s actually far from clear that everyone is equally inclined to free ride on the efforts of others. It’s also not clear that all have as strong a tendency to withdraw effort on seeing that one or more others are contributing less. Some may value the goal more than others, take pride in doing more, or treat the presence of a few slackers as a fact they’re willing to live with provided that the group contains enough cooperators to get the job done.

In a laboratory game, for instance, five people may each be given $10 and asked to divide it between an amount kept private and an amount pooled with the others’ money, tripled, and divided five ways. If all pool their full $10, the combined $50 becomes $150, and divides into $30 for each—a 200 percent profit. If only four put in their $10 and the fifth puts in nothing, the pool has $40, which becomes $120 and each of the five gets $24, which is still 140 percent profit for those who contributed. Would the four contribute $10 each if they knew that it would give each of them $24 instead of the original $10, and that there would be a hold-out who gets the same $24 share and also keeps their own $10, thereby earning $34? Perhaps no. But refusing to contribute, in view of such knowledge, and earning $10 instead of $24 due to unwillingness to be taken advantage of, would be a case of “the best being the enemy of the good.”

Recent Experiment

In recent research, my collaborator Arhan Ertan of Bogazici University (Istanbul) and I invented a variant on the conventional public goods experiment with which to study the conflicts between the desire for joint profit and the resistance to being taken advantage of. Five anonymous players are randomly grouped together, and each gets 10 currency units (CU) in each of 10 periods of play. If any combination of the five puts a total of 110 CU into a joint account, all five receive 10 CU during each remaining period. Earnings are thus highest if each puts their 10 CU into the project in the first two periods and puts in 2 of 10 CU in period three, since they then earn 0 in periods 1 and 2, 18 (their kept 8 plus 10) in period 3, and 20 in each of periods 4 to 10, for a total of 158 CU rather than the 100 CU earned if each simply keeps all CU available to them.

But the players are unable to discuss their situation and unable to form a binding agreement. Predicting what people will do in this situation is nearly impossible, since so much depends on what each believes about one another’s beliefs and motives. One of the most important things one needs, to form a good prediction, is a sense of whether, in the face of evidence that not everyone is doing their “fair share,” any cooperating group members will pull back or quit entirely, versus forging ahead so long as there are enough other cooperators that they can make themselves better off by completing the project despite knowing that some others are “making out like bandits” by free riding on their efforts. With no clear prediction of what would happen, we set out to see what a few hundred study participants would do in fact.

While there is great variation among the outcomes and while our analysis is still ongoing, it’s striking that in not one of the more than 70 groups of five participants studied did most members give up on putting the necessary funds into their group project, although every single group had at least one “slacker,” which caused the benefits of cooperation to be unequally shared. Reaching the target followed different courses in different groups, with 30 percent of them reaching it in the minimum possible time, hence coming close to maximum earnings. The records of the five players’ individual decisions on how much to put into the project, period by period, read like dozens of sagas in which there are always at least one or two acting as if daring the others not to keep going, and often a majority displaying hesitation at one or another point in the process.

The key point, however, is that almost all players ended up improving their earnings—scarcely any earned less than the 100 CU available without project completion, and on average they raised their earnings to more than 142 CU, which is 90 percent of the maximum possible. In a sense, it was only possible because enough members of each group turned out to be willing to live with being taken advantage of a little by whichever group members chose more selfish decisions. Cooperation in spite of some holdouts can occur, and can benefit the vast majority, so refusing to go on because one or two don’t carry their weight was not the main order of the day among these study participants. There may be a lesson from this for both family dynamics and global cooperation.

item.title: AI Presents Answers, But It Is Not the Answer
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Presents Answers, But It Is Not the Answer

The media reports that there is a recommendation AI should interact with children.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Empathy and Theory of Mind are not optional.
  • AI cannot and does not offer genuine emotional presence.
  • Skills, knowledge, and learning mature gradually, and require constant work.
Source: Dee / Pixabay

Recently, there has been conversation in the media to the effect that artificial intelligence (AI) should be used to communicate and engage with children. This advice needs to be considered in light of what the research indicates is taking place. AI cannot and does not offer genuine emotional presence, nor can it model or convey the subtle, unpredictable dynamics of human interactions, nor family nuances or cultural or social complexities (Li & Lee, 2025).

The message is unambiguous: Relying on AI as a substitute for parental or other human engagement risks further displacing the profound experiences children especially need to hear and engage in face-to-face conversations, and years of physical play—at the very minimum—to cultivate healthy, holistic cognitive, emotional, psychological, personal, and social development, including empathy and Theory of Mind.

For empathy and Theory of Mind to develop, constant face-to-face human communication from birth, along with its associated social scaffolding and developmental processes, must unrelentingly take place to bring about the required holistic—brain, mind, and body—healthy, ethical, and complex universal human condition (Li & Lee, 2025).

Skills, knowledge, cognitive and emotional intelligence, empathy, and Theory of Mind are foundational, holistic capacities that begin at birth. When a baby first looks into their mother’s face and eyes and hears their mother’s voice, this marks the start of the all-important forever communication process that begins the journey toward understanding oneself, others, and the external world (Kurian, 2025).

These neurological and learning systems will only mature through ongoing, continuous face-to-face communication, involving constant talking, listening, and observing. The development of empathy and Theory of Mind requires repeated, embodied, i.e., personal reciprocal social experiences that involve facial expressions, tone of voice, gesture, and shared attention; all of which are part of the universal human condition.

As the research indicates, when these experiences are reduced or replaced by digital interaction, the developmental trajectory can change and fail to develop. Critically, prolonged screen‑mediated interaction erodes empathy and Theory of Mind by stripping away the embodied cues that scaffold neurological, psychological, intellectual, emotional and behavioral development.

The evidence is unambiguous: empathy and Theory of Mind are not optional; they are absolute, immutable developmental necessities. Without these intrinsic states being present in the universal human condition, the research indicates that individuals will tend to struggle to interpret nuances, regulate emotion, and successfully engage in cooperative behavior. When these profound states are absent, research indicates that individuals may even engage in behaviors that could be described as being antisocial.

An additional key factor is the absence of personal social learning interactions. This all-important universal personal social learning interaction is the required process of face‑to‑face experiences that helps develop and advance the holistic universal human condition, thereby helping children, adolescents and adults better understand themselves and others.

When this is taking place, there is also the ongoing potential of advancing critical thinking and higher-order reasoning, and it also provides the potential to develop and enhance emotional intelligence, self‑regulation, self-management, self-discipline, and, importantly, ethical and moral intelligence (Kurian, 2025; Li & Lee, 2025; Swarts, 2022).

However, as the research indicates, none of this can or will develop in the “cocoon” of digital environments. As the research also indicates, a digital environment can—and actually does—lead to reduced emotional intelligence, diminished cognitive and intellectual perspective‑taking, and diminished ethical and moral insights, rather than advancing self‑reflective intellectual, ethical, and moral understanding (Chen et al., 2017; Kurian, 2025; Li & Lee, 2025; Soares et al., 2023).

This can also lead to difficulty developing integrity and genuine, stable relationships, which can also reduce tolerance for different points of view, impair conflict-resolution potential, and, as noted, lead to antisocial behaviors (Chen et al., 2017; Kurian, 2025; Li & Lee, 2025; Soares et al., 2023).

At the societal and even broader civilizational level, the implications are profound. A population with no insight into empathy and/or Theory of Mind becomes more susceptible to ethical and moral disengagement. As such, it can even become a danger to itself.

When individuals lack the cognitive, intellectual, emotional, and psychological self‑reflective insight to recognize the emotional and psychological states of others, this is when there is a serious risk of personal relationship failures and also of the broader community becoming socially disruptive, and, as noted, antisocial (Bandura, 1999; Kurian, 2025; Li & Lee, 2025).

For the first time in human history—and it is important to note that this is just the beginning—what we have now in AI is an all-powerful technology that can and does present information faster than humans and, self-evidently, much, much more. As the research indicates, AI “has answers,” but it is not the answer in the development of a holistic, healthy, and ethical universal human condition.

This can only be developed, advanced, and enhanced through constant face‑to‑face human communication. As the research indicates, if this does not occur, the brain and mind of the universal human condition will be adversely affected (Kurian, 2025; Li & Lee, 2025).

Sasha Rogelberg (2026), writing in Fortune, reported that the United States invested more than $30 billion over a 20-year period to expand access to laptops and tablets in schools, broadening access to information and improving learning and educational outcomes.

The evidence accumulated over those 20 years discovered that the widespread introduction of digital devices in classrooms coincided with a measurable decline in students’ academic, cognitive, and educational abilities.

All of the neuroscience, educational, pedagogical, psychological, and learning research unambiguously indicates that for skills, knowledge, empathy, emotional intelligence, and Theory of Mind to develop and advance, this process must begin at birth and continue through sustained, never-ending human interactions.

This involves specific personal learning actions that advance and enhance intellectual and skill acquisition, critical thinking, and higher‑order reasoning from birth through childhood, adolescence, and adulthood.

As such, it is important to note that the brain undergoes continuous major structural changes well into early adulthood, including significant maturational reorganization extending into the late 20s and early 30s. Plus, adult neurogenesis (the formation of new neurons) can continue throughout a lifetime (Gage, 2025; Mousley et al., 2025).

When this essential developmental process is weakened, displaced, or interrupted, the personal and social consequences can become increasingly serious. As noted, this concern, in part, is objectively reflected in the 20‑year study reported by Sasha Rogelberg (2026), which highlights the measurable negative impact that digitally dominated environments are now having on students’ academic and cognitive development. Where to from here?

item.title: The Risks and Rewards of 'Wanderlove'
item.description:
Mating

The Risks and Rewards of 'Wanderlove'

Keep in mind these things before getting tripped up with "wanderlove."

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • "Wanderlove" describes some kind of romantic connection with another person that occurs during travel.
  • Travel can bring you in contact with different people and allow you try new things in a time-limited manner.
  • Keep in mind the risks of wanderlove, though, such as heartbreak and being in unfamiliar situations.
People on social media and the internet are using "wanderlove" to describe a romantic connection that occurs during travel.
Source: PM Images / Getty

Are you wondering if you'll have some "wanderlove" this summer? Well, the rest of August still gives you a fair amount of time to take a trip where you may even fall in love—or at least fall in lust. Such wanderlove could end up making for a memorable trip. Don't get tripped up, though, by not taking the appropriate precautions.

What Is Wanderlove?

"Wanderlove" may sound like "wanderlust," which is having the strong desire to travel. Wanderlust can lead to wanderlove. But this is not a lust-turning-to-love thing in a traditional sense. No, wanderlove is a term that appeared in the list of predicted dating trends for 2023 from the dating app Bumble and has continued to trend on social media and the Internet through 2026 to describe some kind of romantic connection with another person that occurs during travel.

It could be just a one-night stand with that person. Or a two-night stand. Or maybe a however-long-the-trip-lasts stand. This could be a time-and-location-limited thing that ends completely when you return home—sort of what Danny Zuko and Sandy Olsson expected when warbling the song "Summer Nights" with friends, because singing with a chorus of friends is what you always do after wanderlove. Alternatively, a case of wanderlove could end up "greasing" the wheels for further future encounters. Heck, a wanderlove could even make you wonder whether there's some real long-term staying potential with this person—à la the whole plot of the movie "Grease."

What Leads to Wanderlove?

So what about travel specifically may be conducive to a romantic connection? Well, traveling can in various ways make you more attractive. Sure, there are the potential frustrations like jet lag and accidentally packing no underwear or nothing but underwear. But presumably you are enjoying yourself and potentially more relaxed while on travel—especially if it's a vacation. Travel could also help you be freer and more your authentic self—or on the flip side, assume a totally different identity—since you are momentarily getting away from a lot of things that may be holding you back—such as your responsibilities, problems, and the expectations of your family, friends, co-workers, job, and community.

Travel can offer new perspectives as well and, thus, open you up to newer things. It can be a reminder that there is a bigger world out there with a range of different people, ideas, cultures, and things. It could put you in more of an explorer's mode, which could prompt you to, umm, explore Ryū, Katya, Alejandro, Aaliyah, or whoever else you happen to encounter.

Plus, if you are going to a location with hot weather, you may be spending more of your time in less of your clothes. So might other people around you. And that can lead you to be less "clothed off" to possibilities and more in heat in more ways than one.

Finally, there's the "What happens in Las Vegas, stays in Vegas" thinking. It may seem easier to take a bit of a gamble and hook up with someone random when there's a clear end date, a geographic boundary, and no one that you know around you to report your shenanigans to everyone else. And you don't have to be in Vegas to treat it like Vegas.

What Are the Risks of Wanderlove?

Speaking of Vegas, the potential rewards of wanderlove don't necessarily mean that you should take big gambles without minding the potential risks. When your trip does end, you could end up heartbroken or in a, gasp, long-distance relationship. Now, a long-distance relationship can work in the long run, as I've written about previously in "A Funny Bone to Pick." But it does require hard work and effort. Moreover, the travel period may not have given you enough time to assess whether the two of you are truly compatible and, thus, the long-distance and long-term potential.

That brings up another risk of wanderlove—namely, hooking up with someone who may be a complete stranger. That's certainly a risk with other kinds of local dating, like through dating apps, where you don't know what personality issues, entanglements, Chlamydia, and other bad things that person may bring. But being away from your home turf and support structures can leave you particularly vulnerable. On top of that, the whole travel process and being in a new place could trip up your judgment and your red flag-dar.

How Should You Approach Wanderlove?

So just because you are far from home doesn't mean that your body should be far from your head. Try to maintain a proper amount of judgment. How you deal with wanderlove possibilities does depend on your purpose of travel. For example, if you are on a business trip, don't just wanderlove away from your responsibilities.

And you can only wanderlove so far from your true personality. If deep down you are, for example, the type of person who can easily and quickly get stuck on someone like peanut butter on a banana, it may be difficult for you to treat a fling as just a fling. Therefore, to protect yourself, consider consciously setting some appropriate boundaries and taking things slower. Maybe don't have sex until you know some key information like his or her personality, values, background, and name.

All the while, it's important to maintain your PC—meaning your perspective and communication. A summer fling could be just that as long as that's clearly communicated between the two of you. Just make sure that you are both on the same page regarding what you want and what will be expected going forward while you are still in the same location and before you go your separate ways. Miscommunication and misunderstanding can lead your hearts to wander in the wrong direction.

If you do take the aforementioned proper precautions and properly balance the risks and rewards, wanderlove could turn out to be a "wander-ful" thing and maybe even more.

item.title: Professors, Pressure, and Perception
item.description:
Education

Professors, Pressure, and Perception

Professors have options to lighten their workload.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Higher education is a public good beset by contentious debates.
  • Students wish to reduce work and so do professors.
  • The tactics used to reduce work lie on a spectrum.
Source: as-artmedia/Shutterstock

You are in the hands of the Philistines, and, dammit, I sent you there. I am sorry. – Ed Turner in a letter to his son Ted, after learning that Ted had chosen to study the classics (Muson, undated)

Are you back in session yet? - H. A. London, speaking for millions

The disputed value of higher education

The national culture of the United States of America has long comprised ambivalent feelings about higher education. Higher education, and the sophistication that comes with it, is a system of ideas and practices inherited from British, French, and German traditions. The provision of higher education, no one denies this, is one mechanism to breed and reproduce élites, that is, individuals who might, for instance, add an accent aigu to French loan words. The current system of the mass university was preceded by a system of tutors educating young aristocrats. This is a cultural history interesting to contemplate.

The American ambivalence toward higher education comprises a tension between admiration for scholarly work, theoretical knowledge, scientific advances, and rhetorical skill on the one hand and can-do, practical, enterprising creativity and chutzpe on the other. Many admire the self-made businessperson more than the public intellectual, even if the latter is also self-made and not a child of privilege. The learned intelligentsia bemoan the deep well of anti-intellectualism in the wider population, while the practically-minded scorn intellectual hubris. The epigraph, found in a father’s letter to his liberally educated son, is a poignant expression of this attitude.

Surveys tracking trust in higher education and its representatives paint a sobering picture (e.g., Gallup, 2025; 2026). The data not so much suggest ambivalence but polarization. The numbers are discouraging to those who believe that higher education is a public good, not merely a path for individuals to gather credit and accumulate prestige. Interestingly, one’s own educational achievement is not a good predictor of one’s attitude toward higher education. Other, more deeply held, values seem to be in play.

Those who deprecate higher education have a smorgasbord of arguments at their disposal: the contentiousness of scholarly debates, a lack of utility, replicability, intelligibility, or actionability of many findings, the politicization of the intellectual landscape, and the hubris and condescension seen in some corners of the professoriate. I observed earlier that many non-academics seem to think professors do not work hard at all. This sentiment suggests perceptions of unearned privilege. I therefore made a list of what most professors must do to survive and prosper (Krueger, 2023a). It is my impression that professors work harder than ever. While some of their tasks have become easier because of technological advances, there are ever more pressures to outcompete one’s colleagues and to satisfy carnivorous deans and bureaucrats who make a living creating and enforcing additional demands on research and teaching faculty.

Carcavelos beach, before class
Source: J. Krueger

The mitigation of work

How may professors respond to the cascading demands made on them? One response, which garners public attention, is to do fraudulent research. Stories of professors who are caught, dismissed, or sued by their institution become well-known morality tales, particularly so if the professor or their institution are famous. The public’s response shows traces of Schadenfreude and told-you-so satisfaction. Fraud creates serious and visible damage, but this is not my concern today. Here, I ask how instructors can skate on thinning ice without cracking it. My inspiration comes from the stories of – and the hand-wringing over – students’ cheating (Krueger, 2026). What can instructors learn from these students?

To be sure, students have always looked for shortcuts. The prospect of getting desired results while expending less energy is a powerful motivator (Kurzban, 2016). The line separating the permissible from the impermissible is most likely to be crossed when the stakes are high and cutting corners is easy. Not much psychology is needed to understand this. Today, Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools offer tremendous help to today’s students, and we are learning that it is not entirely clear what uses of AI may be classified as cheating. The ethicists are busy trying to figure this out. Their job is difficult since the capabilities of AI have been growing at an accelerating pace.

What of the effort-reducing instructors? What can they do to lighten their workload? They can certainly use AI, a move that can greatly enhance what they offer their students, but a move that also brings the danger of hypocrisy. “I will use AI,” the instructor might declare, “but you mustn’t!” Here now is a tentative top-10 list of shortcuts instructors can use to guard against burnout. I present each shortcut in its most drastic form. Bear in mind that each of these (in)activities lie on a spectrum. Some of these items have a tongue-in-cheek quality to them – and increasingly so as we move down the list.

[1] Flip the lecture class, teach more seminars, avoid laboratory courses. Let students present material and lead discussions. Tell them it is in their own best interest to do so (it actually is, Krueger, 2023b).

[2] Assign your own publications as readings. This cuts down on the preparation time, and students will be reluctant to dispute the work vigorously.

[3] Get teaching assistants (TAs), train them minimally, tell them they grow the most when they train themselves, and then delegate whatever you can to them.

[4] Recruit guest lecturers and visitors eager to discuss their ideas in class.

[5] Go to conferences and give talks elsewhere. Enjoy yourself while out of town.

[6] Show up late and leave early, within reason. Stretch those reasons.

[6] Minimize your accessibility to students. Allow a 50-minute office “hour” per week (except when traveling). Do not respond to emails; there’s that office hour after all.

[8] Take the Socratic method beyond its limits. “I don’t know anything; now, listen to me!”

[9] Get sick and obtain accommodations.

[10] Become a dean or land any kind of bullshit job in the institutional apparat (Graeber, 2018).

I emphasize that this list suggests nothing about how rare or how common any of the listed (in)activities are. The evidence I have seen suggests that most professors and most students work hard and ethically most of the time. Since the use of work-saving tactics among students has been recognized as a pressing concern by instructors, classmates, and family members, parallel questions need to be entertained in regards to instructors’ motivated choices. Otherwise, we run the risk of mistaking our assumptions for truth. For a comprehensive review of tactics and strategies in what is now called “job crafting,” see Demerouti (2026).

Note. I thank Cliff Dutton, Steven Moss, and Ariella Reynolds for critical and constructive comments on a draft of this essay. The views expressed herein are my own.

item.title: Why Genocide Does Not End When the Killings Stop
item.description:
Displacement

Why Genocide Does Not End When the Killings Stop

Twelve years on, Ezidi recovery requires restoring six basic needs.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Genocide destroys not only lives, but the psychological foundations of collective existence.
  • Twelve years later, around 2,600 Ezidis remain missing and over 200,000 displaced.
  • Recovery requires restoring the conditions for safety, agency, belonging, dignity, and continuity.

Between 2014 and 2019, I treated many Ezidis who had fled Shingal, the region internationally known as Sinjar in northern Iraq, after attacks by the Islamic State. They had survived violence, abduction, enslavement, family separation, and displacement.

Yet Ezidis (also spelled Yazidi) who had lived in Germany for decades also came to me in severe distress. Although they had not been in Shingal on August 3, 2014, many experienced fear, helplessness, grief, sleep disturbance, and intrusive images. Some feared that an ancient religious community might disappear before the eyes of the world.

Source: By Sefik Tagay

For centuries, the numerically small Ezidi community has endured massacres, forced conversions, persecution, and displacement across the Middle East. The 2014 genocide reactivated and escalated this historical threat. Its effects can extend across generations through collective memory, family relationships, silence, disrupted cultural transmission, and continuing insecurity.

Twelve years ago today, the Islamic State attacked Shingal. Thousands of Ezidis were murdered, more than 6,000 were abducted, and hundreds of thousands were displaced. Women and girls were subjected to enslavement and systematic sexual violence; boys were separated from their families, indoctrinated, and trained for combat. In 2016, a United Nations Commission of Inquiry concluded that the Islamic State had committed genocide against the Ezidis. In January 2023, the German Bundestag unanimously reached the same conclusion. Legal recognition named what survivors and their families had already lived through.

Our 2017 Lancet study of 512 Ezidis in Germany documented this reach into the diaspora: 25.8 percent screened positive for probable post-traumatic stress disorder, 39.3 percent reported clinically relevant anxiety, and 18.9 percent reported clinically relevant depression. Probable PTSD was more prevalent among women, and elevated distress also occurred among people without direct exposure.

Genocide Targets a People’s Psychological World

Genocide cannot be understood as physical violence alone. It seeks to destroy a group as a group, its relationships, agency, dignity, cultural continuity, and capacity to imagine a future.

We formulated a theory of universal psychological basic needs that identifies six equally fundamental and interdependent needs: safety and predictability; attachment and belonging; autonomy and influence; competence and effectiveness; dignity and recognition; and meaning and coherence. The 2014 genocidal campaign violated all six simultaneously.

Mass killing, captivity, displacement, and uncertainty about missing relatives destroy safety and predictability. Murder, separation, and dispersal rupture attachment and belonging. Abduction, sexual enslavement, forced conversion, and political powerlessness violate autonomy and influence. The loss of homes, education, work, and ordinary roles undermines competence and effectiveness. Dehumanization and humiliation assault dignity and recognition. The destruction of sacred places, the disruption of religious continuity, and assumptions about justice wound meaning and coherence.

Our basic needs theory also helps explain persistent reactions. Hypervigilance may be an attempt to preserve safety; withdrawal may protect against further loss; anger may defend violated dignity; silence may shield relatives from unbearable memories; and testimony may help restore coherence and recognition. Such reactions can be attempts to regulate profoundly violated needs, not just signs of disorder.

The consequences may extend across generations, but such transmission is neither automatic nor biologically predetermined.

Our Lancet study did not directly test intergenerational transmission, and Ezidi-specific evidence about children and grandchildren remains limited. Research across genocide-affected groups and clinical observations suggest pathways: caregiver insecurity, unresolved grief, disrupted emotional availability, family silence or overwhelming narratives, discrimination, continuing displacement, and uncertainty about the community’s future. When caregivers’ own safety, belonging, dignity, or agency remain threatened, meeting these needs consistently in children can become more difficult.

Some younger Ezidis are affected not only by earlier trauma, but by adversity that remains present. Supportive relationships, stable living conditions, recognition, and participation can interrupt these pathways.

The genocide dispersed thousands of Ezidis across the United States, Canada, Australia, and Europe. Germany is home to an estimated 350,000 Ezidis, constituting the world’s largest Ezidi diaspora community. Diaspora can offer safety, education, and participation while also separating families and placing language, oral traditions, and religious continuity under pressure.

The Genocide’s Consequences Remain a Lived Reality

Twelve years after the attacks, approximately 2,600 Ezidis remain missing. More than 200,000 Ezidis remain displaced, many still living in camps. Others have returned to Shingal but lack adequate services, livelihoods, and stable conditions for rebuilding.

These are not merely statistics. Every unresolved disappearance prevents families from knowing, mourning, and rebuilding. Each additional year in displacement prolongs uncertainty, dependency, and loss of influence over the future. The genocidal assault is a historical crime, but psychologically and socially it has not ended as a lived reality.

These continuing conditions help explain why these psychological consequences remain active across individuals, families, and generations: prolonged disruptions of safety, belonging, agency, dignity, and meaning can keep trauma embedded in everyday life. The genocide is therefore not only a past event in collective memory, but an unresolved context of loss, displacement, and threatened continuity.

item.title: Why Conspiracy Theories Are Not Bedtime Stories
item.description:
Conspiracy Theories

Why Conspiracy Theories Are Not Bedtime Stories

Bedtime stories mean to entrance; conspiracy theories mean to entrap.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Conspiracy theories foster mistrust and undermine well-being.
  • This fearful version of storytelling recruits deep mistrust and improbable, stubborn belief and fixation.
  • Conspiracy theories intensify agitation and outrage, engaging suspicion and a sense of betrayal.

Many years ago (so long since, in fact, that I’m tempted to begin this piece with “Once upon a time”), my young daughters demanded nightly episodes of a group of forward-rolling stories under the heading The Wondrous Wise Maharajah of Rajanapour.

I’ll make no apologies for cultural misappropriation. It suffices to say that this far-off kingdom, a kind of Shangri-La, in addition to imaginative transport, required some long travel of the two young girls.

First, they hopped a plane from their home near Niagara Falls, then embarked on a long sea voyage, then boarded a rickety train, then climbed aboard a wagon that followed a rough trail (sometimes the bed would bounce), and then mounted the shoulders of a magical, wisecracking elephant who, in his deep, nasal elephantine voice, answered many questions with open-ended questions of his own.

Now and then the young Maharajah himself was a kind of mountainy Sherlock Holmes, a swordsman who unmasked a pretender to divinity who was frightening his subjects. Or he would solve the seasonal appearance of apparent blood pooling in the corner of a room in a local abode. (Spoiler alert: It was runoff from decaying fallen leaves…) Sometimes the ruler was an adventurer. Once he discovered a thieves’ treasure hoard. Then he put the mountain of gold toward civil engineering improvements in his realm—smooth roads, vast dams, and majestic, sweeping bridges that carried his subjects to the palace.

Despite his skilled storytelling (and he had stories to tell!) the girls had discovered the dashing young Maharajah’s illiteracy, and so taught him to read and write. He, in turn, wielding national policy, hired teachers to teach his kingdom’s young girls and engaged coaches to field women’s soccer teams. And in his old age (picture him as the avatar with a long white beard wearing flowing white robes), he became the founder of one of the world’s great libraries.

In the course of things, the two young girls grew up to occupy offices along the airy colonnade in the kingdom’s research institute. Their tasks, to bring together the world’s prodigious thinkers—scientists, poets, engineers and healers, singers and philosophers—to solve planetary problems.

When the two grown-up ladies made their trips to Rajanapour, sometimes with their own lucky grandchildren in tow, they would, at last and in style, land on the Maharajah’s helicopter pad.

The Maharajah cycle (if I can call it that!) drew from the common elements of storytelling told in the third person. Strong, believable, familiar, empathetic characters drove the narrative. A journey to an exotic place guided the plotlines and gave the author time to improvise and the license to explore. An element of fantasy made the improbable special and achievable. Unexpected fun and adventure cropped up along the way. (A landslide blocks the roadway, and the mighty magical elephant thrusts the rocks aside!) Authorial messaging—beware posers, spellbinders, scoundrels, and thieves—extracted gentle morals that gave the listeners a stake in making a thoughtful future world thrive.

Playful Storytelling vs. Conspiracy Theorizing

Adults do not stop telling stories to others and to themselves. The memory of those entertaining bedtime sessions—driven by creativity with a purpose—has led me to think of the contrast between purposeful, soothing, playful imagination that demands only suspension of disbelief versus the distortions of conspiracy theorizing.

This fearful version of storytelling, hardly a literary genre at all, recruits deep mistrust and improbable, stubborn belief and fixation.

In the “all-seeing eye,” conspiracy theorists detect, hiding in plain sight, evidence of a plot to enslave the world.
Source: de:Benutzer:Verwüstung / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

While the object of the Maharajah cycle was quite literally about peace of mind, currently circulating conspiracy theories (some of them generated and amplified by artificial intelligence) only intensify agitation and outrage, engaging suspicion and a sense of betrayal, and riding on dark resentment.

Conspiracy Theories Are Not Bedtime Stories

Here’s a short list of popular conspiracy theories currently circulating.

For instance: We have been cheated: The moon landing was faked by thieves who stole vast taxpayer funds. We are being misled: Schools abandon cursive instruction to prevent the next generation from reading the United States Constitution. We have been baited and switched: Mind-controlling microchips have been secreted into vaccine injections. We have been victimized: Just who is behind the disappearance of scientists who know the truth of the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic? We have been disenfranchised: The last election was stolen. We have been infected: Agricultural terrorists, fanatic vegetarians, and vegans have released Lone Star ticks whose bite causes allergic reactions to red meat. And one more among many more which are less far-reaching: Climate change science is a hoax propagated by vested interest in electric car technology.

Truth or Consequences

Conspiracy theories prohibit coincidence. That these tales are occasionally laughable (think Bigfoot) matters little for those who embrace them as articles of faith. For devotees, speculation becomes proof and convincing evidence. That kind of certainty comes with a cost.

Leaving aside the effect that the spread of misinformation has had on our waning confidence in public institutions, medicine, and political discourse, psychologists have noted the toll that such strange, unsubstantiated ideas, once spread on social media, take on the personal sense of well-being and life satisfaction of millions of subscribers.

British social psychologists Andrew Denovan and his colleagues, who study adherence to conspiracy theories, have recently noted baleful effects of “threat-based information processing.” These include invasive pessimism, a creeping sense of betrayal, and the oppressive anxiety of “ontological insecurity”—a disturbing feeling of unreality and dislocation. These effects, they note in understatement, are “non-adaptive” as trust in oneself and others erodes.

While a belief that Bigfoot lives a concealed life in the undiscovered north woods is probably innocuous (and surely humorous), the sinister side of conspiracy theory gives rise to concern and alarm. Conspiracy theorizing, the social scientists observe, tends to ascribe unfolding events to “coordinated, purposeful, and covert actions of powerful actors.”

That is, behind breaking news lies the machinations of dark forces that mean us harm and mysterious shadowy groups bent on undermining us.

And so, needing to ascribe blame, basic mistrust, and disappointment easily finds culprits—religious, linguistic, and racial and sexual minorities; migrants; centers of learning and learning itself; and political enemies—thus undermining the foundation of our democratic society and the open discourse it rests upon.

The soothing bedtime story means to send children off to sleep. The conspiracy theory means to frighten and conscript the vulnerable.
